questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Importance of Manufacturing' refers to.
questions.a: Manufacturing is the processing of raw materials into more valuable products; industries that process agricultural, mineral or forest raw materials are called secondary activities, and the economic strength of a country is measured by the development of its manufacturing industries.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Importance of Manufacturing'.
questions.a: Manufacturing industries expand trade and commerce, earn foreign exchange, generate employment and reduce dependence on agriculture, thereby modernising the economy and raising national income.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Importance of Manufacturing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Importance of Manufacturing

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Industrial Location Factors' refers to.
questions.a: Industrial location is influenced by the availability of raw material, labour, capital, power, market and transport; the aim is to minimise the cost of production and deliver goods efficiently to consumers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Industrial Location Factors'.
questions.a: An ideal industrial site minimises production and distribution costs by balancing access to raw materials, power, labour, capital and market; sometimes government policies provide the key incentive.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Industrial Location Factors' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Industrial Location

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Agro-based Industries' refers to.
questions.a: Agro-based industries process agricultural raw materials; the main examples are textile (cotton, jute, silk), sugar and vegetable oil industries, which depend on farm output and are widely spread across India.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Agro-based Industries'.
questions.a: Agro-based industries add value to farm produce, generate rural employment and are located close to the source of their raw material to minimise transport of bulky inputs.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Agro-based Industries' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Agro-based Industries

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Mineral-based Industries: Iron and Steel' refers to.
questions.a: Iron and steel is the basic industry since it provides the base for all other industries; steel is needed for machinery, tools and infrastructure, and the industry uses iron ore, coking coal, limestone and manganese as raw materials.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mineral-based Industries: Iron and Steel'.
questions.a: The iron and steel industry is a heavy, basic industry whose location is governed by the availability of raw materials (iron ore, coal, limestone) and which forms the backbone of industrial development.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Mineral-based Industries: Iron and Steel' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Mineral-based Industries

concepts.title: Mineral-based Industries: Aluminium, Cement and Chemicals

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Mineral-based Industries: Aluminium, Cement and Chemicals' refers to.
questions.a: Other mineral-based industries include aluminium smelting (the second most important metallurgical industry), cement production (needed for construction), and chemical industries (producing inorganic and organic chemicals, fertilisers and pharmaceuticals).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mineral-based Industries: Aluminium, Cement and Chemicals'.
questions.a: Aluminium smelting, cement and chemical industries are mineral-based industries that support construction, transport and agriculture; their location depends on the availability of bauxite, limestone and raw chemicals respectively.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Mineral-based Industries: Aluminium, Cement and Chemicals' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Mineral-based Industries

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Public Sector Industries' refers to.
questions.a: Public sector industries are owned and operated by the government; in India they were set up to provide infrastructure, create employment and reduce regional disparities, while the private sector operates for profit and the joint sector combines both.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Public Sector Industries'.
questions.a: Public sector industries are established in areas where private investment is unlikely because returns are slow, to build infrastructure, ensure equitable development and prevent concentration of economic power.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Public Sector Industries' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Public Sector Industries

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Industrial Pollution and Environmental Degradation' refers to.
questions.a: Industries cause four types of pollution -- air, water, land and noise -- through emissions, effluents, solid waste and machinery, leading to environmental degradation and health hazards.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Industrial Pollution and Environmental Degradation'.
questions.a: Industrial pollution arises because factories emit gases, discharge toxic effluents, dump solid waste and generate noise; the concentration of industries in a few regions worsens the environmental impact.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Industrial Pollution and Environmental Degradation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Industrial Pollution and Environmental Degradation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Control of Environmental Degradation' refers to.
questions.a: Environmental degradation caused by industries can be controlled by treating hot water and effluents before discharge, using smokestacks and electrostatic precipitators, recycling waste, and following pollution-control norms.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Control of Environmental Degradation'.
questions.a: Pollution can be reduced by treating industrial waste, using cleaner technology, fitting particulate-control devices, planting trees and relocating or redesigning factories to minimise emissions.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Control of Environmental Degradation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Control of Environmental Degradation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Industrial Disasters' refers to.
questions.a: Industrial disasters are major accidents in factories causing death, injury and long-term damage; the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) is the worst, caused by a methyl isocyanate leak, and led to stricter safety and disaster-management norms.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Industrial Disasters'.
questions.a: Industrial disasters result from negligence, poor safety standards and hazardous chemicals; the Bhopal tragedy highlighted the need for on-site disaster management plans and strict regulation of hazardous industries.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Industrial Disasters' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Industrial Disasters

questions.a: 54 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Contribution of Industries to the National Economy' refers to.
questions.a: Industries contribute to the national economy by generating employment, producing goods, earning foreign exchange and raising GDP; the share of manufacturing in GDP and the growth rate of output indicate industrial development.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Contribution of Industries to the National Economy'.
questions.a: The contribution of manufacturing to GDP and its annual growth rate measure industrial progress; a strong industrial sector reduces dependence on agriculture and raises national income and employment.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Contribution of Industries to the National Economy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Contribution of Industries to National Economy
